summary:
Mission: LEO — Project Description

The Problem
Real satellite mission design balances orbital mechanics, power, thermal limits, and strict budgets. Existing learning tools are either too abstract (equations), too specialized (expensive professional software like STK or MATLAB), or too passive (articles and videos). As a result, most people lack intuition for how design tradeoffs lead to mission success or failure.

The Solution
Mission: LEO is a browser-based 3D satellite design and orbital simulation game that teaches real aerospace engineering through hands-on play. Players design spacecraft, choose orbits, and manage operations within the 200–2,000 km Low Earth Orbit (LEO) band—the most commercially active region of space.
details:
What does it do / how does it work? Mission: LEO is a browser-based game where players design a satellite from modular components, launch it into Low Earth Orbit, then operate it in real simulated time — aiming cameras at geographic targets, managing power and data storage, waiting for orbital access windows, and downlinking images to ground stations to fulfill mission contracts.

What benefits does it have? It makes satellite mission design intuitive and interactive. Players build genuine engineering instincts — why orbits are chosen, why power budgets fail, why a missed contact window costs a contract — without needing professional software or aerospace training.

Intended impact? To close the gap between public interest in space and real understanding of how missions work. Students, enthusiasts, and early-career engineers can explore design tradeoffs and experience mission operations consequences in a low-stakes, engaging format.

Tools and languages used? Vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the frontend. Three.js for 3D rendering of the satellite, Earth globe, and sensor footprints. A custom J2-perturbed orbital propagator for physics simulation. Browser localStorage for save/resume. No frameworks or backend server required — it runs entirely in the browser.

How is it creative? The physics is real, not approximated for fun. Eclipse periods, ground station contact windows, and imaging access windows are all propagated from actual orbital mechanics models. Cloud cover, wheel faults, and seasonal variation affect whether a capture succeeds. The game respects the player's intelligence and treats failure as the teacher.

Factors considered? Accuracy vs. accessibility — keeping the physics honest without overwhelming new players. Performance in-browser without a backend. Mobile and desktop layout compatibility. Preserving player progress across sessions. Making abstract concepts like orbital ground tracks and sensor swath widths spatial and visible through 3D visualization.
